name: Nevada
summary_text: Travellers entering Nevada are subject to the United States federal document regime. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, recognises only two sexes for federal purposes and directs agencies to implement that binary; the State Department suspended applications for passport gender-marker changes and ended the self-identified 'X' passport option on 22 January 2025. Passports issued before January 2025 carrying a marker other than sex assigned at birth remain valid until expiry, but new applications are processed only as M or F. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in force since 1992.  Entry rules add a separate exposure. Under Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025, trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events are refused visas, with applicants flagged under the internal code 'SWS25'; an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as having committed fraud and barred permanently. Screening at US checkpoints carries an outing risk, since TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy. Several foreign governments have responded to these document and data rules: in April 2025 multiple countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States, and in March 2025 at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for their trans and nonbinary citizens.  Nevada's own framework is protective on identity documents and anti-discrimination. State law bars discrimination on the basis of gender identity and expression alongside sexual orientation. Since 2016 Nevada Vital Records has issued a corrected-gender birth certificate on two affidavits alone, with sex reassignment surgery not required, and comparable changes are available for driver's licences and state IDs. A law signed 22 June 2017 abolished the 1988 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before legal sex changes on government documents. Nevada has offered an 'X' third-gender designation on driver's licences, birth certificates and state IDs since 2019 with no medical documentation required, a state-level option that the federal passport suspension does not extend.  Care access inside Nevada is broader than the federal baseline but constrained at its edges. In March 2018 the state Medicaid agency announced it would cover sex-reassignment surgery, state law bans health insurers from discriminating against transgender patients, and a bill signed in June 2023 requiring insurers, including Medicaid, to cover all medically necessary gender-affirming treatments took effect 1 January 2024. In May 2023 the governor signed a law protecting transgender and intersex individuals in state correctional facilities, while the 2023 omnibus bill SB 302, which would have shielded gender-affirming care and abortion, was vetoed.  A July 2026 national legal risk assessment credits Nevada with fairly robust non-discrimination policies but finds it falls short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people; Nevada sits in the assessment's Low-Risk group (Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia), directly below the most-protective tier.  Federal measures continue to apply inside Nevada regardless of state policy. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals in summer 2025 for full records of patients under 19, specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline were shut down in July 2025, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

name: New Hampshire
summary_text: Visitors to New Hampshire stand under the United States national framework in every respect that touches identity documents and entry. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department no longer processes the X marker, and passports are issued only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted. Passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry, but trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application. The Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to continue this treatment, and the ACLU litigation on behalf of seven plaintiffs is pending.  Entry rules add a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', and an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.  Within that national regime, New Hampshire carries an unusually high recorded incident load. GLAAD's 2025 national census documents 72 anti-LGBTQ incidents in New Hampshire during 2025, the second-highest count of any state after California's 198, and ahead of Texas at 66, Ohio at 50 and Washington at 50. The figure exceeds counts recorded in states with several times New Hampshire's population, which is the strongest single indicator in the sourced material of what a trans visitor may encounter on the ground.  Against that, the state's courts have applied existing civil-rights machinery to a trans victim. On 17 July 2026 the Merrimack County Superior Court found that a Concord man violated the New Hampshire Civil Rights Act by striking a transgender woman. The case establishes that assault against a trans person in New Hampshire can be pursued as a civil-rights violation and adjudicated in state court, rather than going unremedied.  Checkpoint and screening exposure follows national procedure: the National Center for Transgender Equality describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can disclose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation. Multiple foreign governments, including at least eight European countries such as Finland and Denmark, have issued or adjusted travel advisories for trans and nonbinary citizens travelling to the United States.
